cimoliopterus:enwiki:4.title: Cimoliopterus (Discovery of more complete relatives and resulting interpretations)

facts.statement: The genus Cimoliopterus was described by Rodrigues and Kellner in 2013.
facts.quote: authority: Rodrigues & Kellner, 2013

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Cimoliopterus is Pterodactylus cuvieri.
facts.quote: type_species: Pterodactylus cuvieri

facts.statement: Two other species are known: C. dunni, described in 2015, and C. colorhinus, originally described by Seeley in 1870.
facts.quote: subdivision: C. dunni Myers, 2015 C. colorhinus Seeley, 1870

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in areas that are now England and the United States.
facts.quote: Cimoliopterus is a genus of pterosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now England and the United States.

facts.statement: The first specimen was found in the Grey Chalk Subgroup of Kent, England, and described as Pterodactylus cuvieri in 1851.
facts.quote: The first known specimen, consisting of the front part of a snout including part of a crest, was discovered in the Grey Chalk Subgroup of Kent, England, and described as the new species Pterodactylus cuvieri in 1851.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus was among the first pterosaurs depicted as sculptures in Crystal Palace Park during the 1850s.
facts.quote: It was among the first pterosaurs to be depicted as sculptures, in Crystal Palace Park in the 1850s.

facts.statement: A snout found in the Britton Formation of Texas was named C. dunni in 2015.
facts.quote: In 2015, a snout discovered in the Britton Formation of Texas, US, was named as a new species in the genus, C. dunni.

facts.statement: A species from the Cambridge Greensand of England was assigned to Cimoliopterus as C. colorhinus in 2025.
facts.quote: A species from the Cambridge Greensand of England originally assigned to Ornithocheirus was assigned to Cimoliopterus in 2025, as C. colorhinus.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus is distinguished by a premaxillary crest that begins further back on the snout compared to related pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Cimoliopterus can be distinguished from related pterosaurs in features such as having a premaxillary crest that begins hindward on the snout

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus was covered in pycnofibres and had extensive wing-membranes supported by long wing-fingers.
facts.quote: As pterosaurs, Cimoliopterus would have been covered in pycnofibres (hair-like filaments), and had extensive wing-membranes, which were distended by long wing-fingers.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus likely fed by dipping its long jaws into water to catch fish with interlocking teeth.
facts.quote: They possibly fed while flying by dipping their long jaws into water and catching fish with their interlocking teeth.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the premaxillary crests were used to stabilize jaws during feeding or served as display structures.
facts.quote: While some have suggested the premaxillary crests were used to stabilise the jaws while submerged in water during feeding, they may have been used as display structures.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus was likely adapted for long-distance oceanic soaring, supported by fossils found mainly in marine settings.
facts.quote: This kind of pterosaur was probably adapted for long-distance oceanic soaring, which is also supported by their fossils mainly being found in marine settings.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus had limited terrestrial abilities due to short hindlimbs and long forelimbs.
facts.quote: While they may have been proficient in water, their terrestrial abilities were limited due to their having short hindlimbs but long forelimbs.

facts.statement: In 2019, Cimoliopterus was classified in the family Cimoliopteridae within the clade Targaryendraconia, with Camposipterus as its closest relative.
facts.quote: Cimoliopterus was moved to the family Cimoliopteridae within the clade Targaryendraconia in 2019, with its closest relative being Camposipterus.

facts.statement: A single tooth originally reported in the holotype snout had disappeared by the time it was examined in the 2000s.
facts.quote: It was originally reported to preserve a single tooth in the first right tooth socket (at the front of the snout), but this had disappeared when the holotype was examined in the 2000s.

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley placed P. cuvieri in the genus Ptenodactylus in 1869.
facts.quote: In 1869, the British palaeontologist Harry Govier Seeley placed P. cuvieri in the new genus "Ptenodactylus" along with other English pterosaurs known mainly from upper jaws, in an index of specimens in the Woodwardian Museum.

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley placed the species in the genus Ornithocheirus in 1870.
facts.quote: In 1870, Seeley placed the species in the genus Ornithocheirus

facts.statement: Richard Owen assigned the species to the genus Coloborhynchus in 1874.
facts.quote: In 1874, Owen assigned the species to the genus Coloborhynchus.

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer noted similarities between Brazilian crested pterosaurs and English taxa based on fragmentary snouts in 1987.
facts.quote: In 1987, the German palaeontologist Peter Wellnhofer described the new crested pterosaur Tropeognathus from the Santana Formation of Brazil and noted the similarities between it and other newly described Brazilian taxa such as Anhanguera to English taxa that were based on fragmentary snouts, such as the various species assigned to Ornithocheirus.

facts.statement: David M. Unwin used the combination Anhanguera cuvieri in 2001, citing Bowerbank and the snout as the holotype.
facts.quote: In 2001, Unwin also used the combination A. cuvieri, and cited Bowerbank for the name, with the snout as holotype.

facts.statement: Alexander W. Kellner and colleagues established the new genus Aussiedraco based on Australian material previously assigned to Anhanguera cuvieri in 2011.
facts.quote: In 2011, the Brazilian palaeontologist Alexander W. Kellner and colleagues made the Australian material that had been assigned to A. ?cuvieri the basis of a new genus, Aussiedraco

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer stated in 1991 that the genus Ornithocheirus was a wastebin of species from different countries needing clearer definition.
facts.quote: In 1991, Wellnhofer stated that the genus Ornithocheirus had become a "wastebin" of species from different countries, assigned to it on the basis of insufficient characters, and needed clearer definition, and perhaps included several distinct genera.

facts.statement: Alexander W. Kellner and colleagues stated in 2011 that there was no ground for placing O. cuvieri in Anhanguera.
facts.quote: In 2011, the Brazilian palaeontologist Alexander W. Kellner and colleagues made the Australian material that had been assigned to A. ?cuvieri the basis of a new genus, Aussiedraco, and stated that they saw no ground for placing O. cuvieri in Anhanguera.

facts.statement: A sculpture of the pterosaur is shown in a quadrupedal pose with one foot flat on the ground.
facts.quote: One sculpture is correctly shown in a quadrupedal pose, and with one foot flat on the ground.

facts.statement: In 2013, Brazilian paleontologists Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner reviewed species previously assigned to the genus Ornithocheirus.
facts.quote: In 2013, the Brazilian palaeontologist Taissa Rodrigues and Kellner reviewed the species that had so far been placed in the genus Ornithocheirus

facts.statement: In 2015, Timothy S. Myers described the specimen found by Brent Dunn as the holotype of the new species Cimoliopterus dunni.
facts.quote: In 2015, the American palaeontologist Timothy S. Myers described the specimen and made it the holotype of the new species Cimoliopterus dunni

facts.statement: The specific name dunni honors the collector Brent Dunn, who died in 2013.
facts.quote: The specific name honours Dunn, who died in 2013.

facts.statement: In 2025, Rubi V. Pêgas assigned the species O. colorhinus to the genus Cimoliopterus.
facts.quote: In 2025, Pêgas assigned O. colorhinus from the Cambridge Greensand to Cimoliopterus as the new combination C. colorhinus

facts.statement: The genus name Cimoliopterus combines the Greek words for chalk and wing.
facts.quote: This generic name combines the Greek words Kimolia (Κιμωλία), which means "chalk", and pteron, (πτερόν) meaning "wing".

facts.statement: The full translation of the genus name Cimoliopterus is "Cuvier's chalk wing".
facts.quote: In full, the name can be translated as "Cuvier's chalk wing".

facts.statement: The size of Cimoliopterus is difficult to estimate because the available fossils are incomplete.
facts.quote: Because the fossils are incomplete, the size of Cimoliopterus is difficult to estimate.

facts.statement: In 1851, Bowerbank estimated the wingspan of Cimoliopterus cuvieri to be about 16.6 feet.
facts.quote: Bowerbank estimated a wingspan of about 16.6 ft in 1851.

facts.statement: In 2001, Unwin estimated the wingspan of Cimoliopterus cuvieri to be about 3.5 meters.
facts.quote: In 2001, comparing the C. cuvieri holotype specimen with the more complete Anhanguera, Unwin estimated a wingspan of about 3.5 m.

facts.statement: In 2023, Witton and Michel estimated a wingspan of 4 meters for C. cuvieri, noting the estimate was rough due to poor fossil quality.
facts.quote: Witton and Michel gave a 4 m wingspan for C. cuvieri in 2023, but cautioned it was "rough" due to the poor fossils.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus dunni was a mid-sized pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of about 6 feet.
facts.quote: C. dunni would have been mid-sized for a pterosaur, with a wingspan of about 6 ft, according to a press release accompanying its description.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus had large, recurved teeth at the front of the jaws that became smaller and well-spaced towards the back.
facts.quote: The teeth at the front of the jaws were large and recurved, and further back the teeth were smaller, slightly recurved, and well-spaced.

facts.statement: Much of the Cimoliopterus skeleton was pneumatized, filled with air sacs to lighten it.
facts.quote: Much of the skeleton would have been pneumatised (filled with air sacs that lightened it).

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus had forelimbs proportionally enormous compared to its legs, featuring very long wing-fingers.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were proportionally enormous compared to the legs, with very long wing-fingers.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus was covered in pycnofibres and had extensive wing-membranes distended by its wing-fingers.
facts.quote: As a pterosaur, Cimoliopterus would have been covered in pycnofibres (hair-like filaments), and had extensive wing-membranes, which were distended by the wing-fingers.

facts.statement: The snouts of Cimoliopterus species are distinguished from other pterodactyloids by a premaxillary crest that begins further back on the snout.
facts.quote: The holotype snouts of the two Cimoliopterus species share features that distinguish them from other pterodactyloid (or short-tailed) pterosaurs such as a premaxillary crest that begins hindward on the snout

facts.statement: Unlike other toothed pteranodontoids, the snout tips of Cimoliopterus species show only a subtle sideways expansion.
facts.quote: The snout tips of C. cuvieri and C. dunni are only expanded subtly from side to side, unlike the "spoon-like" expansions seen in many other toothed pteranodontoids, such as Anhanguera, Coloborhynchus, and Ornithocheirus.

facts.statement: The holotype of Cimoliopterus cuvieri consists of the front 7 inches of the snout, primarily made of premaxillae and including a premaxillary crest.
facts.quote: The holotype of C. cuvieri is composed of the front 7 in of the snout, represented mainly by the premaxillae, including the premaxillary crest.

facts.statement: Unlike the genus Anhanguera, C. cuvieri does not have its fourth and fifth tooth socket pairs smaller than its third and sixth pairs.
facts.quote: C. cuvieri also does not have its fourth and fifth pair of tooth sockets smaller than its third and sixth, which is a key feature of Anhanguera.

facts.statement: Bowerbank and Owen described and illustrated the now-lost teeth associated with the C. cuvieri holotype in 1851.
facts.quote: Bowerbank and Owen described and figured the now lost teeth found with the C. cuvieri holotype in 1851.

facts.statement: The largest displaced tooth found with the holotype was longer than 1.32 inches, while another was less than 1 inch and located near the third tooth socket pair.
facts.quote: The largest of the displaced teeth was longer than 1.32 in, while the other was less than 1 in, and was found near the third pair of tooth sockets.

facts.statement: Broken tooth tips revealed they were made of compact, hard dentine covered by a thin layer of enamel.
facts.quote: The tips were broken off, revealing they were composed of compact, hard dentine, that was sheathed by a thin coat of enamel.

facts.statement: The enamel of the teeth is marked by fine, longitudinal ridges of unequal length with wide intervals.
facts.quote: Fine, longitudinal ridges (or striations) unequal in length, with wide intervals mark the enamel.

facts.statement: The holotype snout of C. dunni comprises the front 18.5 cm of the snout, including the premaxilla and maxilla with an intact crest, broken just behind the 13th tooth socket pair.
facts.quote: The holotype snout of C. dunni is composed of the front 18.5 cm of the snout, comprising the premaxilla and maxilla (including a largely intact premaxillary crest), broken off just behind the 13th pair of tooth sockets.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of C. dunni preserves a total of twenty-six tooth sockets.
facts.quote: The total number of tooth sockets preserved in the specimen is twenty-six.

facts.statement: C. dunni is distinguished from C. cuvieri by a premaxillary crest that begins at the fourth socket pair and is slightly upwardly curved with a concave front edge.
facts.quote: C. dunni is distinguished by the premaxillary crest beginning at the fourth socket pair, unlike that of C. cuvieri, and the crest is slightly upwards curved, forming a front edge that is concave.

facts.statement: The premaxillary crest in C. dunni is fully fused to the jaw, indicating the individual was not a juvenile.
facts.quote: The crest is fused entirely to the jaw, which indicates the individual was not a juvenile.

facts.statement: If symmetrical, the complete premaxillary crest of C. dunni would have measured approximately 15 to 16 cm in length.
facts.quote: If the crest was symmetrical, the complete crest would have had a length of approximately 15 to 16 cm.

facts.statement: The maximum height of the crest in C. dunni is 38 mm, located above the ninth and tenth tooth socket pairs.
facts.quote: The maximum height of the crest is 38 mm, which is above the ninth and tenth pair of tooth sockets.

facts.statement: The snout tip of C. dunni is blunt.
facts.quote: The tip of the snout in C. dunni is blunt.

facts.statement: The snout width of C. dunni increases backward to a maximum of 1.8 to 1.9 cm at the broken hind edge of the crest.
facts.quote: The width of the snout continues increasing hindward until it reaches a maximum of 1.8 to 1.9 cm at the broken part of the hind edge of the crest.

facts.statement: A narrow palatal ridge less than 1 mm high extends forward from the broken rear end of the premaxillary crest in C. dunni.
facts.quote: At less than 1 mm high, a narrow palatal ridge extends towards the front from the broken portion on the rear end of the premaxillary crest.

facts.statement: C. colorhinus differs from C. cuvieri, which lacks a frontal snout expansion and a depression above the first tooth socket pair.
facts.quote: It differs from C. cuvieri because that species lacks an expansion at the front of the rostrum and a depression aboive the first pair of tooth sockets.

facts.statement: While Seeley speculated the depression above the first tooth pair in C. colorhinus was for lip attachment, Rodrigues and Kellner questioned this in 2013, noting pterosaurs likely had horny beaks.
facts.quote: Seeley speculated that it was the attachment area for lips, but Rodrigues and Kellner questioned this in 2013 because pterosaurs had horny beaks.

facts.statement: It is uncertain whether C. colorhinus had a crest because all known specimens are incomplete.
facts.quote: Since all the specimens are incomplete, it is uncertain if this species had a crest.

facts.statement: In 1870, Seeley classified the species under the name Ornithocheirus cuvieri within a group he named Ornithocheirae.
facts.quote: In 1870, Seeley assigned P. cuvieri (under the name Ornithocheirus cuvieri in his classification) to a group named Ornithocheirae, which consisted only of the genus Ornithocheirus

facts.statement: Species in the genus Ornithocheirus were characterized by sideways compressed beaks with obtuse tips, a palate curving upward and backward, and a longitudinal ridge on the palate.
facts.quote: All the species in the genus Ornithocheirus were diagnosed as having sideways compressed beaks, with the tip more or less obtuse (with an angle over 90°), their palate being curved slightly upward and facing backward (which caused their front teeth to point directly forward), and having a longitudinal ridge on the palate.

facts.statement: In 2001, Unwin considered the species a member of the family Ornithocheiridae along with other Cretaceous pterosaurs from England and Brazil.
facts.quote: In 2001, Unwin considered A. cuvieri a member of Ornithocheiridae, along with many of the English and Brazilian Cretaceous species

facts.statement: In 2013, Witton described the classification of ornithocheirids as controversial and confused due to competing schemes among paleontologists.
facts.quote: In 2013, Witton described the state of ornithocheirid classification as infamously controversial and confused, with competing schemes used by different groups of palaeontologists.

facts.statement: In 2013, Rodrigues and Kellner assigned the species to the group Pteranodontoidea in an uncertain position, forming a sister group to the clade Anhangueria.
facts.quote: In its description by Rodrigues and Kellner in 2013, Cimoliopterus, which consisted only of C. cuvieri, was assigned to the group Pteranodontoidea, though in an uncertain position (incertae sedis), with it and "Ornithocheirus" polyodon forming a sister group to the newly named clade Anhangueria.

facts.statement: In 2019, Pêgas and colleagues included the species in the newly named group Targaryendraconia.
facts.quote: Later in 2019, Pêgas and colleagues redescribed the species Ornithocheirus wiedenrothi as Targaryendraco, and named the new group Targaryendraconia, wherein Cimoliopterus was included.

facts.statement: Further shared features include a palatal ridge extending to the level between the third and second tooth socket pairs and the widest portion of the snout front located at the third pair of tooth sockets.
facts.quote: Further shared features between Cimoliopterus and Camposipterus include the presence of a palatal ridge that extends towards the front until the level between the third and second pair of tooth sockets as well as the location of the widest portion of the front part of the snout, which is at the third pair of tooth sockets.

facts.statement: Myers concluded that the genus is unlikely to be a paraphyletic group based on similarities in jaw form and dentition between C. dunni and C. cuvieri and clear differences from Aetodactylus.
facts.quote: Due to the similarities in the jaw form as well as the dentition of both C. dunni and C. cuvieri, and clear differences from Aetodactylus in these features, Cimoliopterus is unlikely to be a paraphyletic (unnatural) group according to Myers.

facts.statement: In 2018, Longrich and colleagues recovered Aetodactylus and the species as sister taxa, reinforcing their close relationship.
facts.quote: In 2018, a phylogenetic analysis conducted by Nicholas Longrich and colleagues also recovered Aetodactylus and Cimoliopterus as sister taxa, reinforcing their close relationship.

facts.statement: In 2019, Jacobs and colleagues placed the species within Ornithocheiridae as the sister taxon of C. nasutus, forming a polytomy with C. colorhinus and C. sedgwickii.
facts.quote: In 2019, the British palaeontologist Megan Jacobs and colleagues performed a phylogenetic analysis where they placed both C. cuvieri and C. dunni within the family Ornithocheiridae, as the sister taxon of Camposipterus nasutus. In turn, their clade forms a polytomy (an unresolved group) along with the species Camposipterus colorhinus and C. sedgwickii.

facts.statement: A 2022 study confirmed that the family Cimoliopteridae is valid.
facts.quote: A 2022 phylogenetic analysis by Rudah Ruano C. Duque and colleagues also confirmed the validity of Cimoliopteridae.

facts.statement: Alexander Averianov distinguished the family Cimoliopteridae by upper jaw traits and the group Targaryendraconidae by lower jaw traits.
facts.quote: He stated that Cimoliopteridae was distinguished by traits of the upper jaw, whereas the putative sister grouping Targaryendraconidae was distinguished by those of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: In 2025, Pêgas supported the validity of Cimoliopteridae based on traits like a nose-like protrusion above the first tooth sockets and a palatal ridge extending between the second and third tooth pairs.
facts.quote: Pêgas supported the validity of Cimoliopteridae in 2025, listing common traits such as a "nose-like" protrusion at the front of the rostrum above the first tooth sockets and the front end of the palatal ridge reaching between the second and third pair of tooth sockets.

facts.statement: Rodrigues and Kellner suggested in 2013 that the crest of Cimoliopterus evolved independently from that of anhanguerids due to its different position.
facts.quote: Due to the more hindward positioned premaxillary crest of Cimoliopterus, unlike those seen in anhanguerids, Rodrigues and Kellner suggested in 2013 that their crests could have evolved independently from each other.

facts.statement: The discovery of Cimoliopterus dunni in North America showed that European and North American pterosaur faunas were similar in the mid-Cretaceous despite the widening Atlantic Ocean.
facts.quote: In 2015, Myers stated that the discovery of C. dunni in North America extended the distribution of the genus Cimoliopterus, showing that the pterosaur faunas of Europe and North America were similar by the mid-Cretaceous despite the ongoing widening of the North Atlantic Ocean.

facts.statement: Myers proposed that pterosaurs moved between continents by island-hopping over fluctuating sea levels rather than using a land bridge.
facts.quote: Myers did not suggest the presence of a land bridge between the continents, but that the sea level fluctuated over time, and pterosaurs could have island-hopped between the land masses that emerged between.

facts.statement: It remains debated why no close ties exist between North and South American pterosaurs, suggesting a possible dispersal barrier.
facts.quote: However, it still remained a mystery why no close ties had been identified between pterosaurs of North and South America, indicating there could have been a barrier to their dispersal.

facts.statement: Pêgas and colleagues agreed in 2019 that the Cimoliopterus crest evolved independently because its closer relatives lacked crests.
facts.quote: In 2019, Pêgas and colleagues agreed with Rodrigues and Kellner that the crest of Cimoliopterus had evolved independently from those of anhanguerians, since closer related targaryendraconian taxa, such as Barbosania, Camposipterus, and Aetodactylus, did not possess crests.

facts.statement: Researchers found the jaw expansion in Aetodactylus and Cimoliopterus unclear as a precursor to the rosette-like jaws of anhanguerians.
facts.quote: Pêgas and colleagues thought the slight sideways expansion in the jaws of Aetodactylus and Cimoliopterus differed from the rosette-like condition seen in the jaws of anhanguerians, and that it was unclear if the condition in the former group was a precursor stage to that of the latter, with this issue needing further investigation.

facts.statement: Witton and Michel noted in 2023 that Cimoliopterus was among the last toothed pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Witton and Michel noted in 2023 that Cimoliopterus has the distinction of being among the last toothed pterosaurs.

facts.statement: In 2006, André J. Veldmeijer and colleagues noted that the interlocking teeth of ornithocheirids were built for spearing slippery prey like fish rather than cutting.
facts.quote: André J. Veldmeijer and colleagues pointed out in 2006 that apart from ornithocheirids usually being found in deposits associated with water, their interlocking teeth also supported piscivory (fish-eating), being built for spearing slippery prey rather than cutting or slashing.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that because their teeth were not adapted for chewing, these pterosaurs might have pre-digested small fish before swallowing, a process requiring cheeks or throat pouches reported in some pterosaurs.
facts.quote: They may have hunted small fish or pre-digested them before swallowing (since their teeth were not adapted for chewing), but the second option would have required cheeks or throat pouches to keep prey inside the mouth; the latter has been reported in some pterosaurs.

facts.statement: Witton considered pterosaur crests to be display structures rather than stabilizers, as they are thought to be sexually dimorphic in some species.
facts.quote: Instead of being used for stabilisation during skimming or flight, Witton considered the crests of pterosaurs to have been display structures, as the crests are thought to have been sexually dimorphic in some species.

facts.statement: Ornithocheirids' terrestrial locomotion was likely limited by short legs, restricting them to slow shuffling walks or faster bounding, indicating they spent limited time on the ground.
facts.quote: Their terrestrial locomotion was probably limited by their short legs, and they may have been restricted to slower shuffling walks (so that the long forelimbs did not outpace the hindlimbs) and faster bounding, which indicates they may have spent limited time on the ground.

facts.statement: Like pterosaurs in general, ornithocheirids probably took flight by launching quadrupedally and were possibly able to swim well enough to take off from water surfaces.
facts.quote: As has been hypothesised for pterosaurs in general, they probably took flight by launching quadrupedally, and they were possibly able to swim fairly well to be able to take off from water surfaces.

facts.statement: Palmer used a structural model with a 6 m wingspan based on CT scans to infer the membrane tension needed to suppress aeroelastic flutter and prevent structural failure during high-speed flight.
facts.quote: He used the bending strength of the wing spar of a structural model with a 6 m wing span based on the CT scans to infer the likely tension of the wing membrane needed to suppress aeroelastic flutter (instability caused by air resistance) at high flight speeds, and minimising ballooning, thus preventing structural failure of the membrane under flight loads.

facts.statement: Palmer's estimates implied the membrane had high-modulus material, supporting the idea that the actinofibril layer reinforcing pterosaur wings was keratinous, similar to human hair and nails, differing greatly from bat membranes.
facts.quote: The three estimates were of similar magnitude, implying the membrane would have high-modulus material (Young's modulus, tensile elasticity), which supports the idea that the actinofibril layer (structural fibres inside the wings of pterosaurs) on the outside of the membrane which reinforced pterosaur wings were of keratinous material (the same material in human hair and nails), and differed greatly from the membranes of bats.

facts.statement: The holotype of C. cuvieri was found in Kent, England, in chalks and marls of the Grey Chalk Subgroup dating to the Cenomanian-Turonian ages of the Upper Cretaceous, though its precise stratigraphic position is unknown.
facts.quote: The holotype of C. cuvieri was found in Kent, England, collected in chalks and marls of the Grey Chalk Subgroup, which dates to the Cenomanian-Turonian ages of the Upper Cretaceous, though the precise stratigraphic position of the specimen is unknown.

facts.statement: The holotype of C. dunni was found in the Britton Formation of north-central Texas, dating to the Cenomanian stage of the early Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The holotype of C. dunni was found in the Britton Formation of north-central Texas, which dates to the Cenomanian stage of the early Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The area where C. dunni was found would have been offshore in the shallow Western Interior Seaway, which covered the central part of the US and Canada.
facts.quote: The area it was found in would have been off shore in the shallow Western Interior Seaway, which covered the central part of the US and Canada.

facts.statement: The genus Cimoliopterus was established by Rodrigues and Kellner in 2013.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Rodrigues & Kellner, 2013

facts.statement: James Scott Bowerbank named and described the type species Pterodactylus cuvieri in 1851 from fossils found in a limestone quarry near Maidstone, Kent.
facts.quote: En 1851, James Scott Bowerbank nombró y describió algunos restos hallados en una cantera de caliza en Burham cerca de Maidstone en Kent, como una nueva especie de Pterodactylus: Pterodactylus cuvieri.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, NHMUK PV 39409, was found in the Chalk Formation dating from the Cenomanian to Turonian stages.
facts.quote: El holotipo, NHMUK PV 39409, fue hallado en una capa de la Formación Chalk que data de entre el Cenomaniense al Turoniense.

facts.statement: The holotype originally preserved a single tooth at the tip of the snout, but this tooth disappeared by 2007.
facts.quote: Originalmente preservaba un único diente en la punta del hocico, pero este desapareció por el año 2007.

facts.statement: A new species, Cimoliopterus dunni, was described in 2015 from the Britton Formation in north-central Texas, USA.
facts.quote: En 2015, se describió una nueva especie, Cimoliopterus dunni de la Formación Britton en el centro-norte de Texas, Estados Unidos

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus is a pteranodontoid closely related to Aetodactylus, which is also found in Cenomanian strata in Texas.
facts.quote: El análisis filogenético de la descripción de esta especie indica que Cimoliopterus es un pteranodontoideo cercanamente relacionado con Aetodactylus, también hallado en estratos cenomanienses de Texas.

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus lived during the Cenomanian to Turonian stages, approximately 100.5 to 89.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Turonian (100.5 to 89.8 million years ago)

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus is an extinct genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur found in England and the United States.
facts.quote: Cimoliopterus es un género extinto de pterosaurio pterodactiloideo de Inglaterra, y Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Rodrigues and Kellner identified two unique derived traits for Cimoliopterus: its crest is located far forward on the premaxilla at the level of the seventh tooth pair but starts before the large nasoantorbital fenestra.
facts.quote: En 2013, Rodrigues y Kellner establecieron dos rasgos únicos derivados o autapomorfias, para Cimoliopterus, que lo diferencian de sus parientes: su cresta se sitúa muy lejos en el premaxilar, al nivel del séptimo par de dientes, pero empieza antes de la fenestra nasoantorbitalis, la gran baertura en el cráneo

facts.statement: Cimoliopterus exhibits a unique combination of general traits including a crested snout, a mid-palatal ridge reaching the third tooth pair, an upwardly curved palate, a lack of anterior mandibular expansion, and second and third tooth pairs being equal in size and larger than the fourth pair.
facts.quote: Aparte de esto Cimoliopterus muestra una combinación única de rasgos más generales: el hocico tiene una cresta; el borde en la zona media del paladar en el frente alcanza el nivel del tercer par de dientes; el paladar se curva hacia arriba; carece de una expansión de la mandíbula en el frente; el segundo y tercer par de dientes son igual de grandes y mayores que el cuarto par de dientes

facts.statement: In the posterior part of the jaw, the distance between the teeth increases gradually.
facts.quote: En la parte posterior la distancia entre los dientes se incrementa gradualmente.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of C. dunni consists of a partial face preserving alveoli for 26 teeth, a thin premaxillary crest starting above the fourth alveolus, a blunt snout tip, and a snout forming a 45° angle with the anterior palate.
facts.quote: El espécimen holotipo consiste en un rostro parcial que preserva los alvéolos de 26 dientes y posee una delgada cresta premaxilar que inicia sobre el cuarto alvéolo, una punta del hocico roma y el rostro forma un ángulo de 45° con respecto a la parte anterior del paladar.

facts.statement: Rodrigues and Kellner assigned Cimoliopterus to the group Pteranodontoidea in an uncertain position (incertae sedis).
facts.quote: Cimoliopterus fue asignado por Rodrigues y Kellner al grupo Pteranodontoidea, en una posición incierta (incertae sedis).

facts.statement: Cladistic analyses indicated a position in the evolutionary tree above Istiodactylus but below a polytomy formed by more derived species.
facts.quote: Los análisis cladísticos indicaron una posición en el árbol evolutivo superior a la de Istiodactylus pero por debajo de una politomía formada por especies más derivadas.

facts.statement: The genus name Cimoliopterus is derived from Kimolia, the white limestone of the island of Kimolos, and the Latinized Greek term pteron, meaning "wing."
facts.quote: El nombre de género se deriva de Κιμωλία, Kimolia, la caliza blanca de la isla Kímolos (kimolia significa "caliza" en griego) junto al término griego latinizado πτερόν, pteron, "ala".

facts.statement: It is debated whether Ornithocheirus brachyrhinus and Pterodactylus fittoni belong to the same taxon as C. cuvieri due to shared characteristics, but Rodrigues and Kellner considered them nomina dubia because they are too incomplete for definitive referral.
facts.quote: Ornithocheirus brachyrhinus Seeley 1870 y Pterodactylus fittoni Owen 1859 comparten varias características con C. cuvieri, y por tanto no se puede excluir que sean parte del mismo taxón. Sin embargo, son demasiado incompletos como para ser referidos definitivamente a C. cuvieri, por lo que Rodrigues y Kellner los consideraron nomina dubia.

facts.statement: In 1851, Bowerbank estimated the wingspan of P. cuvieri to be nearly 5.04 meters, making it the largest known living or extinct flying animal at that time.
facts.quote: Bowerbank, haciendo extrapolaciones a partir de los restos de P. giganteus, estimó que la envergadura de P. cuvieri sería de cerca de 5.04 metros, lo cual lo convierte el animal volador de mayor tamaño vivo o extinto conocido en 1851.
